title: High Efficiency in Large Supercurrent Rectification with Superconducting Coil
authors: Takumi Ichikawa, Daisuke Takegami, Gen Nishijima, Shunsuke Kawakami, Tsutomu Nojima, Yuji Tsuchiya, Satoshi Awaji, Fuyuki Ando, Ken-ichi Uchida, Yuya Hattori, Yoshikazu Mizuguchi
abstract: Superconducting diodes (SDs) are devices that rectify supercurrent through the difference in the superconducting critical current (Ic) between forward and reverse current directions. For bringing such SDs closer to practical superconducting power electronics applications, a combination of both high rectification efficiency (η) and a large Ic difference (ΔIc) is required. Here, we propose and demonstrate a coil-shaped superconducting wire device concept to induce a large SD effect, arising from the compensation between an external magnetic field (Hext) and the field generated by the coil itself. From transport Ic measurements on coil-shaped SDs based on a Sn10-Pb90 solder wire, we achieved a η of 79% with a ΔIc of 140 A at Hext = 500 Oe (coil #2) and a η of 84% with a ΔIc of 125 A at Hext = 530 Oe (coil #3), confirming high rectification values at large supercurrents. The large-current high-efficiency SDE in the coil-shaped SDs will be highly useful for developing the potential field of supercurrent power electronics.
summary: This work introduces a coil-shaped superconducting wire device to enhance supercurrent rectification (SDE) for power electronics. By engineering the coil geometry, the device achieves high rectification efficiency ($\eta$) and a large critical-current difference ($\Delta I_c$) under significant external magnetic fields. The combination of FEM simulations and precise transport measurements validates this approach for next-generation superconducting power applications.
main_problem: The goal is to achieve high rectification efficiency ($\eta$) and a large critical-current difference ($\Delta I_c$) simultaneously in superconducting diodes (SDs) for practical superconducting power electronics.
main_result: The proposed coil-shaped superconducting wire device demonstrated high performance, achieving $\eta = 79\%$ with $\Delta I_c = 140 	ext{ A}$ at $500 	ext{ Oe}$, confirming its potential for large-current applications.
method: The study combines experimental transport measurements (V-I curves) with detailed Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics to model the magnetic field distribution.
model_or_system: The physical system is a coil-shaped superconducting wire (initially $	ext{Sn}_{10}	ext{-Pb}_{90}$ solder), where the Superconducting Diode Effect (SDE) arises from the non-reciprocity of the critical current due to the interaction between an external magnetic field ($	ext{H}_{	ext{ext}}$) and the field generated by the coil itself.
key_observables: Rectification efficiency ($\eta$), critical-current difference ($\Delta I_c$), and the superconducting critical current ($I_c$) dependence on $	ext{H}_{	ext{ext}}$.
important_parameters: External magnetic field ($	ext{H}_{	ext{ext}}$) up to $530 	ext{ Oe}$; superconducting critical field ($H_c$) for $	ext{Sn}_{10}	ext{-Pb}_{90}$ solder ($\approx 570 	ext{ Oe}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on classical electromagnetism for modeling, and the performance is highly dependent on the magnetic field at the inner edge of the coil.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic designs, photographs of the coil diodes, and plots detailing the magnetic field distribution ($H_{total}$) and the dependence of $I_c$ on $H_{ext}$ derived from both simulation and experiment.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for high $\eta$ and $\Delta I_c$. It then presents the coil concept, supported by FEM simulations showing how field compensation leads to non-reciprocity. Finally, it reports experimental measurements on improved coil designs, confirming the high performance metrics.
why_interesting: While focused on classical superconducting electronics, the detailed modeling of non-linear, field-dependent critical currents and the use of advanced electromagnetic simulations are relevant to understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in condensed matter systems.
